title: Forward Bloc, INA and Independence and Partition
tagline: Quit India, the Forward Bloc, the Indian National Army, the missions and the road to partition and freedom.

overview.intro: The last dozen years of British rule contained the most violent and the most diplomatic phases of the freedom movement at once: an unarmed mass revolt in 1942, an armed Indian army that fought under a captured flag, and a series of missions and plans that ended with the transfer of power and the partition of the country. This chapter works through Quit India and the repressive response to it, the founding of the Forward Bloc and the career of Subhas Chandra Bose and the Indian National Army, and then the constitutional diplomacy — Cripps, the Shimla Conference, the Cabinet Mission, Direct Action and the Mountbatten Plan — that produced independence on 15 August 1947 along with the two dominions of India and Pakistan. The examination habit for this chapter is chronology in order: an answer that names the missions in the wrong sequence loses its argument.

facts.label: Quit India
facts.value: The Congress session of August 1942 at Bombay passed the Quit India resolution; Gandhi said do or die, and the entire Congress leadership was arrested within hours.

facts.label: The Forward Bloc
facts.value: Founded by Subhas Chandra Bose in May 1939 after his resignation as Congress President, to rally left-wing and socialist opinion.

facts.label: The INA
facts.value: The Indian National Army, first led by Captain Mohan Singh and Rash Behari Bose, then reorganised by Subhas Chandra Bose as the Azad Hind Fauj.

facts.label: Transfer of power
facts.value: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 created two dominions, and freedom came on 15 August 1947 with partition.

learningOutcomes: Explain the causes and conduct of the Quit India movement of 1942 and the government’s repression.
Describe the founding of the Forward Bloc and Subhas Chandra Bose’s role in the Indian National Army.
Trace the sequence of constitutional proposals from Cripps 1942 to the Mountbatten Plan of 1947.
Explain the growth of the demand for Pakistan and the events leading to Direct Action and partition.
State the main provisions of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and assess the meaning of 15 August 1947.

blocks.text: By 1942 the war had reached the borders of India, with Japanese forces in Burma and the Andamans under occupation, and the failure of the Cripps Mission convinced the Congress that nothing would be conceded without pressure. The Working Committee met at Wardha in July 1942 and the All India Congress Committee met in Bombay in August, where on 8 August 1942 the Quit India resolution was passed demanding an immediate end to British rule. Gandhi addressed the session with the words do or die, and within hours the government struck: on the night of 9 August the entire Congress leadership — Gandhi, Nehru, Patel, Azad and the provincial leaders — was arrested, and the Congress and its newspapers were declared unlawful. What followed was a revolt without central direction: in Bihar and eastern UP the students and the Congress Socialist Party members took over administration for short periods, in Ballia and Tana Bhagat areas the British authority briefly collapsed, the Gujarat mills stopped, and parallel governments functioned at Ballia, Satara and Tamluk. The government responded with mass arrests, machine-gunning from aircraft in some districts, punitive fines, the withholding of compensation and the dismissal of the press. The movement was over as an organisation by the end of 1943, but it had destroyed the myth of British invincibility and made it clear that India could not be held by consent after the war.

items: The Cripps Mission of March 1942 offered dominion status after the war and was rejected as a post-dated cheque in a crashing bank.
The Quit India resolution was passed at Bombay on 8 August 1942, with Gandhi’s do or die as its watchword.
The leadership was arrested on the night of 9 August 1942 and the Congress and its press were declared unlawful.
The revolt was spontaneous and local: parallel governments at Ballia, Satara and Tamluk, strikes in the mills of Gujarat and student action in Bihar.
Repression included arrests by the thousand, firing, punitive fines, dismissal of officials and heavy censorship.
The significance: the end of reliance on British goodwill and the clear proof that the Raj could not survive a determined mass movement.

learn.title: The Forward Bloc, Subhas Chandra Bose and the INA

blocks.text: Subhas Chandra Bose, elected Congress President in 1938 and again in 1939 with Gandhian support contested by the official candidate, resigned after differences with the Working Committee and in May 1939 founded the Forward Bloc as a left-wing alternative within the nationalist family, with the aims of the complete independence of India, the attainment of socialism, the ending of imperialist alliances and the release of political prisoners. Interned in his own house during Quit India, he escaped in January 1941, travelled through Kabul and Moscow to Germany, and from Berlin broadcast and organised an Indian Legion. In 1943 he took command of the Indian National Army in South-East Asia: the INA had begun in 1942 with Indian prisoners of war under Captain Mohan Singh with Japanese encouragement, was revived by Rash Behari Bose, and under Subhas Chandra Bose, who reached Singapore in July 1943, it was reorganised as the Azad Hind Fauj with the slogan Delhi Chalo and the war cry Jai Hind, with the Rani of Jhansi Regiment of women under Captain Lakshmi Sahgal. The INA marched into India in 1944 through Imphal and Kohima and was defeated by the monsoon, the supply lines and the British and Indian armies, and Bose died in an air crash in August 1945 in Formosa. The INA trials of 1945 at the Red Fort, where Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon were court-martialled, were followed by such public sympathy that the government dropped the cases, and the loyalty of the Indian armed forces to the Crown was never again beyond question.

items: The Forward Bloc was founded by Bose in May 1939 with the aims of complete independence, socialism and anti-imperialism.
Bose escaped house arrest in January 1941 and reached Germany, where he broadcast and raised an Indian Legion.
The INA began in 1942 with prisoners of war under Captain Mohan Singh, was led next by Rash Behari Bose, and reached its final form under Subhas Chandra Bose from July 1943.
The Azad Hind Fauj adopted Delhi Chalo and Jai Hind and included the Rani of Jhansi Regiment of women under Captain Lakshmi Sahgal.
The 1944 campaign into Imphal and Kohima failed on supply and the monsoon, though it shook British confidence.
The Red Fort trials of 1945 provoked nationwide sympathy and made the loyalty of the Indian forces uncertain, which hastened the transfer of power.

blocks.text: Constitutional diplomacy after Quit India moved through four proposals, and examiners expect them in order. The Cripps Mission of March 1942, sent to secure Indian cooperation in the war, offered dominion status after the war with the right of provinces to opt out of a future union, and was rejected by the Congress as a post-dated cheque in a crashing bank and by the League as unsatisfactory. The Shimla Conference of 1945, between the Viceroy Lord Wavell and the Congress and the League, broke down because the League insisted on nominating all Muslim members of the Executive Council while the Congress insisted on including Muslim League members who were also Congressmen. The Cabinet Mission of 1946 proposed a three-tier federation — a centre with defence, foreign affairs and communications, grouped provinces in three groups, and provincial autonomy — with an interim government, and it was at first accepted by both parties before Jawaharlal Nehru’s press conference remark on the optional nature of the groups led the League to withdraw. The Attlee government then announced the transfer of power by June 1948, sent Lord Mountbatten as Viceroy, and the Mountbatten Plan of June 1947 partitioned British India into two dominions with the Punjab and Bengal divided, and independence was fixed for 15 August 1947.

items: Cripps, March 1942: dominion status after the war with provincial option, rejected as inadequate by both the Congress and the League.
Shimla, 1945: broke down over the League’s demand to nominate all Muslim members of the Executive Council.
Cabinet Mission, 1946: a three-tier federation with a strong centre, grouped provinces and provincial autonomy, plus an interim government.
The mission plan was first accepted, then wrecked by the disagreement over the grouping of provinces and the League’s withdrawal.
Direct Action Day, 16 August 1946, was called by the League for Pakistan and was followed by communal killings at Calcutta and elsewhere.
The Mountbatten Plan of June 1947 accepted partition and fixed 15 August 1947 as the date of the transfer of power.

learn.title: The growth of Pakistan and the partition

blocks.text: The demand for Pakistan grew out of the Muslim League’s analysis that in a united India Muslims would be a permanent minority, and out of the failures of the 1937 provincial elections, when the League formed no government despite offers, which convinced Jinnah that the Congress could not be trusted to share power. The Lahore Resolution of March 1940, moved by Fazlul Huq and supported by Jinnah and the Choudhuries, asked for independent states for the Muslim-majority areas in the north-western and eastern zones, and this became the Pakistan demand. The Direct Action Day of 16 August 1946, called to press the demand, led to the Great Calcutta Killing and to retaliatory violence in Noakhali, Bihar, Punjab and elsewhere, so that the transfer of power was planned under the shadow of civil war. The Mountbatten Plan of June 1947 accepted partition, the Punjab and Bengal were divided by boundary commissions chaired by Sir Cyril Radcliffe, the Indian Independence Act, 1947 created the two dominions with effect from 15 August 1947, and the partition was accompanied by one of the largest migrations in history, with communities uprooted and a great loss of life and property. Radcliffe’s boundaries were announced after independence, which is one of the bitter ironies of the transfer.

items: The 1937 elections and the League’s exclusion of government in the provinces convinced Jinnah that power would not be shared.
The Lahore Resolution of March 1940 asked for independent states in the Muslim-majority north-western and eastern zones.
Direct Action Day, 16 August 1946, produced the Great Calcutta Killing and retaliatory violence in Noakhali, Bihar and the Punjab.
The Mountbatten Plan of June 1947 accepted the division of British India into two dominions.
The Punjab and Bengal were divided by boundary commissions under Sir Cyril Radcliffe, whose awards were published after 15 August 1947.
The Indian Independence Act, 1947 created the two dominions, and partition brought the largest migration in history and a great loss of life.

learn.title: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the meaning of 15 August 1947

blocks.text: The Indian Independence Act, 1947, passed by the British Parliament in July 1947, gave effect to the Mountbatten Plan. It created two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947, with the right to frame their own constitutions and to remain within or leave the British Commonwealth. Each dominion was to have a Governor-General to represent the King, and the princely states were left free to accede to either dominion or, in theory, to remain independent — a provision that produced the delayed accession of Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir. The Constituent Assembly of each dominion was to function as the legislature until a new constitution was framed, the existing laws were to continue until altered, and the forces were to be divided between the two dominions. In India, Jawaharlal Nehru became the first Prime Minister, Lord Mountbatten the first Governor-General and Dr Rajendra Prasad the first President of the Constituent Assembly, and independence was celebrated at midnight on 14 to 15 August 1947 with the tricolour raised and Nehru’s Tryst with Destiny speech. Freedom was therefore achieved in two senses at once: the end of foreign rule, and the beginning of a national task — a constitution, the integration of the states, the healing of partition and the making of a secular democracy — which the following years had to complete.

items: Two dominions, India and Pakistan, were created with effect from 15 August 1947, each free to frame its own constitution.
Each dominion had a Governor-General, and Lord Mountbatten served as the first Governor-General of India.
The princely states were left free to accede, which made the integration of Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir necessary.
The Constituent Assembly of each dominion acted as its legislature until a constitution was framed.
Forces, civil services, assets and liabilities were divided between the two dominions.
India celebrated freedom at midnight with the tricolour and Nehru’s Tryst with Destiny address; partition accompanied the celebration.

items.note: Nehru’s midnight speech of 14 to 15 August 1947, which described the hour of freedom as the end of a chapter and the birth of a nation’s soul.
Junagadh acceded to Pakistan, Hyderabad delayed, and Kashmir acceded after invasion — each showing the weakness left by the Act’s silence on the states.

blocks.text: The last phase is best assessed by asking what each strand contributed to the transfer of power. Quit India destroyed the pretence that British rule rested on Indian consent: the scale of the revolt and the severity of the repression made it clear that a post-war Britain could neither govern nor justify governing India. The INA and the Forward Bloc supplied the nationalist challenge with a dimension of armed sacrifice, and the Red Fort trials made the loyalty of the Indian armed forces uncertain, which mattered more to the calculations of the Attlee government than any resolution of the Congress. The constitutional missions supplied the legal route, and the failure of the Cabinet Mission plan shifted the choice from a united federation to partition, which the Mountbatten Plan then executed quickly. The limitations of the phase should be named too: the Congress accepted a partition it had opposed for twenty years, the transfer was rushed in a way that cost hundreds of thousands of lives and uprooted millions, and the princely states were handled without a settled principle until military and diplomatic action integrated them. The verdict is that independence was won by the combination of mass pressure, armed example and diplomatic timing, and that its price — partition — became the first and hardest problem of the free nation.

items: Quit India ended the myth of consent and made post-war British rule impractical.
The INA and the Red Fort trials shook the loyalty of the armed forces, which the Attlee government could not ignore.
The missions supplied the constitutional route, and the failure of the Cabinet Mission plan made partition the working option.
The Indian Independence Act, 1947 created two dominions and left the states free to accede.
The limitations: acceptance of partition, the haste of the transfer and its human cost, and the unsettled position of the princely states.
Verdict: freedom was won by mass pressure, armed example and diplomatic timing, and partition became its first great problem.

items.note: Take each strand — mass movement, INA, missions — and say what it achieved, then close with the cost of partition and the unfinished work of integration.

questions.prompt: Describe the events of Quit India between 8 August and the end of 1942.
questions.answer: The All India Congress Committee met in Bombay on 8 August 1942 and passed the Quit India resolution, with Gandhi’s do or die as its watchword. Within hours, on the night of 9 August, the entire Congress leadership was arrested and the Congress and its newspapers were declared unlawful. The movement then became spontaneous and local: students and Socialists took over administration in parts of Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, parallel governments functioned briefly at Ballia, Satara and Tamluk, the mills of Gujarat stopped and the railways and communications were attacked. The government replied with mass arrests, firing, punitive fines, censorship and the dismissal of officials, and by 1943 the organisation of the movement was crushed although its spirit was not.
questions.explanation: The resolution, the arrests of 9 August, the local revolts and parallel governments, and the repression are the four parts.

questions.prompt: State two aims of the Forward Bloc and two features of the Indian National Army under Subhas Chandra Bose.
questions.answer: The Forward Bloc aimed at the complete independence of India and at the attainment of socialism, and it stood against imperialist alliances and for the release of political prisoners. The INA under Bose was reorganised as the Azad Hind Fauj with the slogans Delhi Chalo and Jai Hind, and it included the Rani of Jhansi Regiment of women under Captain Lakshmi Sahgal; the force marched into India towards Imphal and Kohima in 1944.
questions.explanation: Two aims of the Bloc and two features of the reorganised INA.

questions.prompt: Mention two provisions of the Indian Independence Act, 1947.
questions.answer: The Act created two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, with effect from 15 August 1947, each free to frame its own constitution and to remain in or leave the Commonwealth. Each dominion was to have a Governor-General, the princely states were left free to accede to either dominion, and the Constituent Assembly of each dominion was to act as its legislature until a new constitution was framed.
questions.explanation: Any two of the two dominions, the Governor-General, the freedom of the states to accede, and the Constituent Assembly as legislature.

questions.prompt: Explain the causes and consequences of the Quit India movement of 1942.
questions.answer: The causes were the immediate danger of Japanese advance into India after the fall of Rangoon and the occupation of the Andamans; the failure of the Cripps Mission of March 1942, which offered dominion status after the war but nothing during it, and which was rejected as a post-dated cheque in a crashing bank; four years of war with rising prices, scarcity and the arrests of Congress leaders for individual satyagraha; and the belief that British rule could not survive a determined mass challenge. On 8 August 1942 the All India Congress Committee passed the Quit India resolution with Gandhi’s do or die, and on the night of 9 August the entire leadership was arrested and the Congress declared unlawful. The consequences were a spontaneous revolt without central direction: parallel governments at Ballia, Satara and Tamluk, strikes in the Gujarat mills, student action in Bihar, attacks on communications and severe repression including firing and punitive fines. In the longer term the movement destroyed the myth of British invincibility, proved that the Raj could not rest on consent, and convinced the Attlee government that power must be transferred; it also left the Congress leadership imprisoned for much of the rest of the war, which allowed the Muslim League to organise without challenge.
questions.explanation: Causes must include the war situation and the failure of Cripps; consequences must cover the revolt, the repression and the long-term effect on British calculations.

questions.prompt: Assess the contribution of the Indian National Army to the achievement of Indian independence.
questions.answer: The INA’s contribution was less military than political, and it operated in three ways. First, it gave the nationalist demand an example of armed sacrifice by Indians under their own flag, with the slogans Delhi Chalo and Jai Hind and the Rani of Jhansi Regiment of women, which revived morale after the mass repression of Quit India. Second, the campaign of 1944 into Imphal and Kohima, though it failed on supply lines and the monsoon, showed that Indian soldiers could and would fight the British, which made the loyalty of the Indian armed forces a live question for the first time. Third, and most directly, the Red Fort trials of 1945 of Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon provoked nationwide sympathy, with the Congress adopting their defence and public collections for their families, so the government dropped the cases; the Attlee government concluded from this that it could no longer rely on Indian troops to hold India. Against this it must be said that the INA was defeated militarily, that it depended on Japanese support for its existence, and that the transfer of power was decided by British calculations after the war rather than by the INA’s battlefield record. The balanced verdict is that the INA turned a political demand into a situation in which repression would be paid for in the loyalty of the army itself, which hastened the decision to leave.
questions.explanation: Three channels of contribution — morale, the loyalty question and the trials — plus the limitations, closing with a verdict on why the British concluded they could not stay.

questions.prompt: How did the demand for Pakistan grow between 1937 and 1947, and what did partition cost?
questions.answer: The growth began with the elections of 1937, when the Congress formed ministries in most provinces and refused a coalition with the Muslim League, which convinced Jinnah and the League that in a united India Muslims would be permanently excluded from power. The Lahore Resolution of March 1940 converted that analysis into a territorial demand for independent states in the Muslim-majority north-western and eastern zones, and the League used its leverage during the war, rejecting the Cripps offer and negotiating alone at Shimla in 1945. The failure of the Cabinet Mission plan in 1946 — the Congress and the League could not agree over the grouping of provinces — and Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946, which produced the Great Calcutta Killing and retaliatory violence in Noakhali, Bihar and the Punjab, made partition the working option for a government determined to transfer power quickly. The Mountbatten Plan of June 1947 accepted the division, the Radcliffe award divided the Punjab and Bengal, and the Indian Independence Act created two dominions on 15 August 1947. The cost was enormous: the largest migration in history, with millions uprooted and a great loss of life, the loss of Lahore and Dhaka’s hinterlands to two countries, a permanent security question on both sides, and the delay of the constitutional work of integration and reconstruction.
questions.explanation: The sequence from 1937 to 1947 must be told in order, and the cost must cover migration, communal loss, security and the delay to nation-building.
